title: Source Diversity for Rare Cuneiform Sign Recognition
tagline: For a rare sign, is one more training example worth more if it comes from a new tablet?
abstract: Cuneiform sign-recognition models learn from crops cut out of photographed clay tablets, and rare signs may have only a handful of examples. Crops from the same tablet share a scribe, clay, lighting and photograph, so simply counting examples per class can overstate how much a model has to learn from. This project asks how much one extra training crop of a rare sign is worth for recognition on unseen tablets, depending on where it comes from: a tablet already in training, a new tablet, a tablet from another site, or an augmented or synthetic copy. It uses the public electronic Babylonian Library (eBL) Sign Snippets release, with tablet-disjoint splits, matched training conditions and paired seeds, and keeps a reserved test set untouched until the design is final.

stats.label: recall on unseen tablets when the same 8 examples per sign come from 8 tablets instead of 2
rare signs improved, with the gain holding in all 3 paired seeds
precision rose too: the model recognized the signs rather than just predicting them more often

compare.title: Recall on unseen tablets, same 8 examples per sign

findings: Same budget, more tablets, better recognition. Spreading 8 training crops per sign across 8 source tablets instead of 2 raised recall on unseen tablets from 12.7% to 19.5% for 30 Old Babylonian signs (ResNet-18, 20,891 crops from 337 tablets).
No cost elsewhere. Accuracy on the other 167 classes was unchanged (72.1% vs 71.8%).

The training protocol matters. With random initialization and a constant learning rate, the model barely learned the 8-example signs and the difference could not be distinguished from zero; the effect appeared with ImageNet-pretrained weights and cosine learning-rate decay.
Open question: part of the benefit may come from photographic variety, such as clay colour and lighting, rather than scribal hand. This pilot can't separate the two yet.

title: Conformal Prediction Under Distribution Shift
tagline: What happens to a coverage guarantee when the world changes?
abstract: Split-conformal prediction gives regression models finite-sample, distribution-free prediction intervals with a guaranteed coverage rate, but the guarantee relies on the calibration and test data being exchangeable. This project asks a direct question: what happens to that coverage guarantee when the test distribution no longer matches the calibration distribution? Using synthetic nonlinear regression data with a known ground-truth function, we build 90% split-conformal intervals, confirm they behave correctly with no shift, and then deliberately introduce three kinds of distribution shift — covariate shift, noise shift, and subgroup (mixture) shift — to measure how badly empirical coverage degrades. We then test four candidate fixes: recalibrating on the shifted distribution, calibrating per subgroup, using a larger calibration set, and changing the base regression model. Recalibration and group-specific calibration both restore coverage close to nominal, but recalibration does so by inflating interval width dramatically, exposing a coverage-vs-usefulness trade-off that is easy to miss if only coverage is reported.

stats.label: coverage under strong covariate shift, against a 90% target
wider intervals needed to restore coverage by recalibration (3.84 → 28.0)
coverage kept by group-specific calibration where pooled drops to 73.3%

findings: Coverage must always be read next to interval width. Both successful fixes restore coverage, but only by widening intervals, sometimes up to 7× under large covariate shift.

Knowing the structure of the shift beats brute-force recalibration. Group-specific calibration restores coverage without runaway width growth, because it only widens intervals for the subpopulation that needs it.
nextSteps: Implement weighted conformal prediction (Tibshirani et al., 2019), which reweights calibration residuals by an estimated likelihood ratio and doesn't need fresh labeled data from the shifted distribution.
Implement adaptive conformal inference (Gibbs & Candès, 2021) for settings where the shift is gradual rather than a single step change.
Replace fixed-width intervals with conformalized quantile regression or normalized scores, so interval width adapts to local difficulty.
Repeat every shift sweep over multiple random seeds and report confidence bands, not single point estimates.
Move from synthetic data to a real dataset with a natural train/test shift.
